What does a just energy transition really look like in practice in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

In a school in Banja Luka, energy efficiency renovations have cut energy use by nearly half — making classrooms warmer, brighter, and easier to maintain for more than a thousand students and staff. Small changes like these signal a deeper transformation underway across the country.

In a new op-ed, "A Shared Just Energy Transition," I share why this transition is not only an energy shift, but one of the largest shared development opportunities for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Three priorities stand out:
🔹 Strengthen governance to unlock finance in renewables. Bosnia and Herzegovina's transition will require over $6 billion in investment, with the grid at the centre. With the Electricity Law and the National Energy and Climate Plan in their final stage of approval, the foundations are in place to mobilize bankable pipelines and innovative financing.

🔹 Transform coal regions into jobs, skills, and growth. Coal still employs 15,000 to 20,000 people directly and supports more than 150,000 jobs across related sectors. Repurposing mine land in Zenica, Banovići, and Kreka — with around 27 MWp of solar capacity planned — shows how existing infrastructure can be turned into productive economic assets when connected to a national innovation ecosystem.

🔹 Harness data, AI, and digital innovation to scale energy efficiency. Public buildings retrofitted through UNDP's Green Economic Development programme have already reduced energy use by 30 to 50 percent. With smart meter deployment already exceeding the 80% national target, accelerating their full use can unlock real-time data, dynamic tariffs, and stronger system resilience.

As UNDP , we stand ready to support this whole-of-system transformation by helping connect policy, finance, and technology to build resilience, create jobs, improve quality of life, and position Bosnia and Herzegovina at the forefront of the next generation of energy innovation.
